title: Lightning Is 5x Hotter Than the Sun's Surface ⚡ #shorts
description:
A lightning bolt heats the air around it to about 30,000 °C (roughly 50,000 °F) in a fraction of a second – about five times hotter than the Sun's visible surface, which is around 5,500 °C. The air expands so violently that it creates a shock wave: thunder. Lightning flashes about 44 times every second worldwide, the longest flash ever recorded stretched 829 km (515 miles) across the US Great Plains in 2017, and the glowing channel is only a few centimeters wide.

Sources: NOAA National Weather Service, NOAA SciJinks, NOAA NSSL, NASA, World Meteorological Organization (WMO), BBC Science Focus

scenes.text: When lightning strikes, it heats the air around it in a tiny fraction of a second.
That air can reach about thirty thousand degrees Celsius. That's around fifty thousand Fahrenheit.
scenes.label: LIGHTNING AIR

scenes.text: The surface of the Sun? Only about fifty-five hundred degrees.
The air expands so violently that it explodes outward. That shock wave is the thunder you hear.
And this happens about forty-four times every single second, somewhere on Earth.
scenes.label: FLASHES PER SECOND

scenes.text: The longest flash ever recorded stretched eight hundred twenty-nine kilometers, from Texas almost to Kansas City.
The twist? That super hot channel is only a few centimeters wide. About as wide as your thumb.
